newsitem.title: USA: Innovative U.S. shopping mall hits milestone.
newsitem.headline: Innovative U.S. shopping mall hits milestone.

text.p: Kansas City civic leaders and revellers launched a giant birthday bash Friday to mark the 75th anniversary of the first U.S. shopping centre designed to accommodate the automobile.

As organisers planned to roll out an oversized birthday cake and shoot off fireworks, Kansas City's "Country Club Plaza" was praised by real estate specialists as a model development that successfully and artfully married two American passions: shopping and driving.
The Plaza opened in 1922 as the brainchild of Jesse Clyde Nichols, a well-travelled entrepreneur who anticipated the massive change that the automobile would have on commerce in the 20th century.

Michael Beyard, vice president of strategic development for the Urban Land Institute in Washington D.C., said the Plaza -- a series of elegant, Spanish-style buildings criss-crossed by wide streets -- is one of the most well-designed shopping centres in America.

"I would say the fact that it is celebrating its 75th birthday shows how this shopping centre was brilliantly conceived, brilliantly executed and has been able to maintain its market position for such a long period of time. This is extremely unusual for a shopping centre," Beyard said.

Scattered across the Plaza's 55 acres are 187 stores and restaurants, 44 statues and fountains and a replica of the Giralda clocktower from Seville, Spain. Amid smaller boutiques are upscale stores like Brooks Brothers, Saks Fifth Avenue, Emporio Armani and Ralph Lauren.

Part of what distinguished the Plaza was its creator's desire for a unique architectural theme to adorn commercial and residential properties. Nichols was so impressed by his travels in Spain that he chose a Moorish motif that included stucco buildings, red-tiled roofs, ornate towers and picturesque courtyards.

But it was Nichols' insistence on including plenty of free parking that spelled long-term success for the Plaza. Nichols believed the car was more than a passing fad and predicted it would become the single most important mode of transportation for years to come.

"The Plaza integrated parking and it integrated access into a very pedestrian-oriented shopping environment. This was a strategy that went out of vogue for decades after the rise of the regional, enclosed mall," Beyard said.

"Now we're seeing a return to street, pedestrian-oriented shopping among many newer shopping centres, and the Country Club Plaza did it the right way all along," Beyard said. "Now they're cutting-edge again."
It's quite a legacy for a development that was initially ridiculed by Nichols' contemporaries.

The land Nichols planned to use was relatively far from Kansas City's bustling downtown district and was nothing more than a dumping ground with a hog farm and a brickyard. About 30 rundown shacks covered the area and stagnant water filled the swampy land.

"It was called 'Nichols' Folly' because this was so far south of the city at that point that people figured no way would people move into homes this far out and shop in this area," said Beth Morrison, a spokeswoman for the Plaza Merchants Association.
But what the city's leaders failed to see was a development that was to become the first master-planned shopping centre in the United States designed with the car in mind.
